# years: A paragraph counts as Siberian if it names a place from the gazetteer lying in one of these regions: Western and Eastern Siberia, the Arctic coast, Yakutia and the North-East, the Amur region, Primorye and Sakhalin, Kamchatka and Chukotka, and also the Steppe region (Akmolinsk and Semipalatinsk provinces). If a paragraph names no places, it takes the region of the previous paragraph in the same chapter

# years: The corpus includes books by authors from European countries outside the imperial centre of Russia, written on the basis of their own journey or residence in Siberia. The country in the filters is the author's cultural and linguistic affiliation, not subjecthood: for #–# these are different things. Russian travelogues belong to a separate corpus; the voices of the Siberian peoples themselves are absent from the corpus, and this is the main limitation of any conclusions about “perception”

The node “natives (generic)” in the network is an effect of the category itself: travellers used the word for any indigenous group, so it is linked to all of them

# years: The images were found in Internet Archive scans (a program selects pages with graphics, crops them and rotates landscape plates) and taken from Project Gutenberg HTML editions, where the captions are typeset. Captions of scans are OCR text of the original and may contain errors; type, peoples and places are derived from the caption; where the caption names no place, the region is taken provisionally from the adjacent paragraph. Each image links to its source and to the paragraph next to it in the library. Images are credited to the book they come from: draughtsmen, engravers and photographers named on the plates have not yet been recorded. How to read the division into “portraits” and “people”, and why photographs of convicts and anthropological “types” are shown as historical documents, is explained on the page
